subject: english
chapter_title: A Letter to God: Faith, Hope and Human Kindness

concepts.title: Lencho's Hope and the Promise of Rain
concepts.definition: Lencho, a farmer who knows his fields intimately, waits for a downpour that will ripen his corn, and he reads the first fat raindrops as new coins promising a good harvest.
concepts.key_idea: The house on the crest of the low hill looks over the river and the field of ripe corn, setting up the contrast between hope and the coming disaster.
question_patterns: what did lencho hope for
why did lencho say the raindrops were like new coins
describe the setting of lencho's house in the valley
how did lencho read the coming weather in the sky
why was the downpour important for lencho's field
what comparison did lencho draw between raindrops and money

solution_steps.explain: Confirm the solitary house on the crest of a low hill with the river and the field of ripe corn below.
Note Lencho watching the north-east sky for clouds and calling the falling drops new coins.
Link the promised shower to a good harvest, which is exactly what Lencho hopes for.

concepts.title: The Hailstorm and the Ruined Crop
concepts.definition: The rain turns violent when a strong wind drives large hailstones that destroy the entire crop, leaving neither flower nor leaf on the corn, so Lencho faces a year without harvest.
concepts.key_idea: The locusts would have left more than the hail, Lencho says, and the field looks as if covered with salt, showing the completeness of the loss.
question_patterns: how did the rain change and what happened to lencho's fields
what were lencho's feelings when the hail stopped
why did lencho compare the destroyed field to salt
describe the destruction caused by the hailstorm
what was the single hope left in lencho's house
how does the story show conflict between humans and nature

solution_steps.explain: Follow the shift from sweet rain to strong wind and large hailstones.
The hail covers the field as with salt, destroying flower, leaf and promise of harvest.
The family consoles itself that no one dies of hunger, and Lencho's single hope turns to help from God.

concepts.title: The Letter to God and the Postmaster's Reply
concepts.definition: Lencho writes a letter addressed simply 'To God', asking for a hundred pesos to sow the field again, and the postmaster answers it by collecting money from employees and friends to protect the farmer's faith.
concepts.key_idea: The postmaster signs the reply 'God' after gathering a little more than half the sum, an act of kindness meant to keep a man's belief alive.
question_patterns: why did lencho write a letter to god
what did lencho ask for in his letter
how did the postmaster answer lencho's letter
why did the postmaster decide to reply to the letter
how much money did lencho request and why
what does the postmaster's act reveal about him

solution_steps.explain: Lencho asks for a hundred pesos to resow the field and to live until the crop comes.
The postmaster, first amused then moved, collects money from post office employees and sends it signed as God.
The reply aims to protect Lencho's faith in God, showing the postmaster's amiable and generous nature.

concepts.title: Lencho's Anger and the Irony of 'Crooks'
concepts.definition: Lencho is neither surprised nor grateful; finding only seventy pesos, he blames post office employees as a bunch of crooks and asks God to send the rest without passing through their hands.
concepts.key_idea: The story ends in irony: the very people who helped Lencho are accused by him, showing his unquestioning but blind faith.
question_patterns: was lencho surprised to find a letter with money
what made lencho angry at the end of the story
why did lencho call the post office employees crooks
how much money did lencho receive and what did he expect
explain the irony in the ending of a letter to god
what kind of a person is lencho

solution_steps.explain: Lencho receives seventy pesos instead of the hundred he asked for, and shows no surprise at getting a reply from God.
He attributes the missing thirty pesos to post office employees and demands the balance be sent by other means.
The helpers stand accused by the helped, exposing the blindness of unquestioning faith and the kindness of ordinary people.

concepts.title: Faith, Conflict and the Story's Message
concepts.definition: The story poses the question of what faith we should place in things, contrasting Lencho's unquestioning faith in God with quiet human kindness, and it runs two conflicts at once: people against nature and people against people.
concepts.key_idea: Faith can move mountains, says the introduction, but the story gently asks whether that faith should rest in the divine alone or also in fellow humans.
question_patterns: describe the two kinds of conflict illustrated in the story
what is the message of a letter to god
are there people like lencho in the real world
how does the story question what we put our faith in
compare lencho's faith with the postmaster's kindness
why is the title a letter to god apt for the story

solution_steps.explain: Nature ruins Lencho's crop, and human suspicion pits Lencho against the post office staff.
Lencho's absolute faith in God drives the plot, while the postmaster's deed answers faith with human help.
The story suggests that kindness of ordinary people often carries out the work that faith expects of heaven.
